title: Antonelli struggling with ‘very difficult’ new-spec car
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has conceded that driving Mercedes’ upgraded car in Singapore – amid the team’s decision to split specifications – proved to be a struggle during Sprint Qualifying, with the Italian labelling his version of the W17 as “very difficult” after ending the session in P7.

The Silver Arrows confirmed ahead of the action getting underway at the Marina Bay Street Circuit that George Russell would revert to the Azerbaijan-specification of the car for the event, while Antonelli would continue to run the upgrade that the team brought last time out in Malaysia.

This decision – on a weekend where Russell will serve a grid penalty due to an unavoidable engine change – was made due to the results from the updates at Sepang proving inconclusive.

As such, Antonelli and Russell completed the opening day of action in Singapore with varying specifications – and it was Russell who led the way on the timesheets, the Briton setting the fastest lap in Friday’s sole practice hour before going second-quickest in Sprint Qualifying.

Antonelli, meanwhile, appeared to be off the pace of his team mate and had to settle for seventh place in both sessions.

Asked after Sprint Qualifying if he was surprised by how difficult it had been to get lap time out of the car, the championship leader responded: “Yes and no, to be fair. Already [in] FP1 I was struggling and, yeah, still a lot to understand about this package.

“The car is very difficult, very unpredictable and very difficult to put a lap together. So yeah, it's a shame because I was coming [here] with high hopes, but so far it's been very difficult."

Given the apparent difference in pace between the two Mercedes specifications so far at Marina Bay, Antonelli acknowledged that the rest of the event could prove challenging for him.

“I think it's going to be a difficult weekend, unless we can pull something out tomorrow,” he explained. “But other than that, it's going to be very tricky. I don't really see where we can find seven tenths, but you never know.

“Maybe tonight, Bono [Pete Bonnington, Antonelli’s race engineer], the engineers, we're going to find something in the car. And for sure, I'm going to try to improve a little bit the driving, and then we'll see tomorrow where we end up.”

title: Russell reacts to P2 in Sprint Quali with downgraded car
excerpt:
George Russell bounced back from the disappointment of his late-race retirement at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia with a strong run to second place during Sprint Qualifying in Singapore, as he reverted to an older-specification car.

After struggling to assess the upgrades they introduced at Sepang, Mercedes have split their approach for the Marina Bay weekend, with Russell going back to the package he drove to pole position and victory in Baku, and team mate Kimi Antonelli keeping the new parts.

That appeared to work in Russell’s favour on Friday, as the Briton charged his way to P2 on the grid for the Sprint – behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen – while the Italian wound up seventh, more than half a second adrift.

Asked about how his Sprint Qualifying session came together, Russell reflected: “I think we’ve seemed competitive all day, to be honest, from the first laps in FP1 – we obviously topped the timesheets there.

“We knew Max was fast, and he went on a slightly different strategy to us in Q3, just doing the one lap. Who knows what was best, but I’m pretty satisfied with the P2.”

As for Mercedes’ split car specifications, and whether any more answers are emerging, he added: “Well, I can definitely confirm the old one is not bad!

“Let’s see what tomorrow brings with Kimi on the upgrade. As a team, there’s still nothing telling us that it isn’t working, but it’s a sport driven by the stopwatch, and the stopwatch has not been great for the upgrade yet.”

Russell, who will take an engine-related grid drop for Sunday’s Grand Prix, then offered a few words on the Sprint race, and if the start will be his best chance of overhauling Verstappen – should the Dutchman keep P1 on the grid amid an investigation for allegedly overtaking Lewis Hamilton under yellow flags in SQ1.

“It’s going to be very challenging,” said Russell. “The grip left to right [on the grid] here is a big difference. The drivers on the pole side last year had a big advantage, so it’s probably going to be trying to maintain P2.

“I know Max is under investigation for the yellows, so let’s see.”

title: Verstappen clinches pole position for Singapore Sprint
excerpt:
Max Verstappen clinched pole position for the Singapore Sprint, beating Mercedes’ George Russell and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in a busy session under the lights at the Marina Bay Circuit.

With four teams seemingly in the mix after a single hour of Free Practice, Verstappen timed his final lap to perfection to eclipse the efforts of each of his rivals, ending the session with a time of 1m 31.156s.

His lap on the soft tyres left him 0.120s clear of Russell, with Leclerc a further tenth back in P3, but the Dutchman’s result will not be confirmed until he has visited the stewards for a potential yellow flag infringement in SQ1.

The McLaren pair of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris took P4 and P5 respectively, with the Aussie just 0.055s adrift of Leclerc’s time. Lewis Hamilton was sixth in the second Ferrari ahead of Kimi Antonelli – the leader of the Drivers’ Championship – and Racing Bull's Liam Lawson.

Isack Hadjar and Pierre Gasly completed the top 10 for Red Bull and Alpine with both having lap times deleted in SQ3.

Alpine’s Franco Colapinto finished in P11 after a late lap from Russell knocked him out of the top 10, while the Audi of Nico Hulkenberg followed in P12. Ollie Bearman (Haas), Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi), Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) and Esteban Ocon (Haas) occupied P13 to P16 on the timesheets.

Arvid Lindblad, who previously hinted he would approach this weekend cautiously after crashing at other street circuits, narrowly missed out on a spot in SQ2 and settled for P17, just ahead of Aston Martin’s Lance Stroll.

They enjoyed a margin of half a second over Williams and Cadillac, with Alex Albon leading the backmarkers in P19 as Valtteri Bottas tucked in just behind. Carlos Sainz will line up on the back row with Sergio Perez for Saturday’s 21-lap affair, the Mexican having caused a red flag after finding the barrier in the opening minutes.

AS IT HAPPENED

SQ1 – Verstappen sets the pace as Perez crashes

The Marina Bay Circuit’s bumpy surface and humid weather make it one of the greatest tests on the calendar, and the addition of the Sprint creates an even greater challenge. It meant that after just one hour of Free Practice, it was time for Sprint Qualifying, with Russell heading into the session as the driver to beat.

When SQ1 got underway under the lights – with everyone set to run the mandatory medium tyres – Cadillac led a long queue of cars out of the pit lane as the drivers prepared to tackle vastly different conditions compared to FP1.

It didn’t take long for the first yellow flag to be waved after Perez crashed into the tyre barrier at Turn 4, damaging his front wing. In an attempt to make it back to his garage, he dragged the component under his car and sent debris flying onto the racing line, resulting in a pause in the action with six minutes remaining.

As everyone returned to the pits under the red flag, only a handful of drivers had set a representative time, suggesting that there would be a frenetic conclusion to the first segment of Sprint Qualifying. Of those, Hamilton led the timesheets with 1m 33.748s – around 1.5s adrift of Russell’s fastest lap in FP1.

Replays also showed that Verstappen – one of the many yet to complete a competitive lap – seemed to overtake the Ferrari under yellow flags, which was noted by the stewards and will be investigated after the session.

With the clock rapidly ticking down, the majority opted for a single push, which unsurprisingly led to a flurry of improvements in the final minutes. Leclerc surged into P2 behind his team mate, followed by the Mercedes pair before Audi’s Hulkenberg snatched P4.

Norris was the next to move into the top three, but the second McLaren of Piastri bailed out of his first effort and faced immense pressure to deliver as he lingered near the drop zone. Although the Red Bulls were in a similar situation, Verstappen was able to post the quickest time of 1m 33.477s, with Hadjar and Piastri also progressing.

At the other end of the order, Lindblad was knocked out alongside Stroll and Williams’ Albon (P19), who reported that the car felt "completely different to practice”, and Sainz (P22). It was another early exit for Cadillac too, Bottas in P20 while Perez wound up in P21.

Knocked out: Lindblad, Stroll, Albon, Bottas, Perez, Sainz

SQ2 – Ferrari fly as Russell delivers under pressure

With every team bolting on the medium compound once again, Verstappen flirted with the walls on his way to setting an early benchmark of 1m 32.724s, making the most of the track evolution to significantly trim his earlier time.

That was initially enough for him to clear Mercedes’ Antonelli and Russell, but Hamilton’s first attempt saw him overturn the Dutchman’s advantage before Leclerc went even faster, posting a 1m 32.457s.

Hamilton reported that “a couple of big snaps” towards the end of the lap made him lose some time, suggesting that there was more performance for the Ferrari driver to find. Someone else chasing improvement was Russell, who suffered a lock-up and had no choice but to go again on his suboptimal tyres, hoping to move up the order from P8.

Hadjar charged into fifth place as Lawson and Colapinto also advanced, demoting Russell into the elimination spots. However, he managed to wrestle his car into P4 when it mattered, sending the Alpine driver down to P11.

Colapinto therefore missed the cut for the final segment of Sprint Qualifying, as did Hulkenberg, Bearman, Bortoleto, Alonso and Ocon.

Knocked out: Colapinto, Hulkenberg, Bearman, Bortoleto, Alonso, Ocon

SQ3 – Verstappen secures pole with last-gasp lap

The light turned green at the end of the pit lane for the final shootout, but Ferrari, Red Bull and the remaining midfield stars of Lawson and Gasly elected to bide their time and wait in their respective garages for a little longer.

That gave Norris the space he needed to push the soft tyres to their limit and take the top spot with a 1m 31.587s, with Piastri close behind in P2 as neither Mercedes could take the fight to McLaren.

Leclerc came through to beat Norris by just 0.019s, and despite Hamilton’s best efforts, the lap time fell away from him and he could only manage P3. There was still just about enough time for Red Bull to blow everyone out of the water, which is exactly what Verstappen did in the first sector.

He carried that speed throughout the rest of the lap to seize pole position for the Sprint, with no one able to beat his final time of 1m 31.156s. Russell came closest for Mercedes and was followed by Leclerc, Piastri and Norris.

Hamilton ended up half a second adrift in sixth ahead of Antonelli, while Lawson, Hadjar and Gasly rounded out the top 10.

Key Quote

"It’s always close here in Singapore," Verstappen said. "Also your lap itself – you’re pushing as hard as you think is possible, close to the walls in places. For sure, once we bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more, but I did not expect this. Of course, very happy to be first."

What's next

With the grid decided, the drivers will line up for the Sprint at 1700 local time on Saturday. Head to the RACE HUB to find out how you can catch the action.

title: Russell beats Leclerc and Norris in sole Singapore GP practice
excerpt:
George Russell finished fastest in Free Practice 1 ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix, the Mercedes driver beating Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris to the top spot.

The Briton posted a 1m 32.274s, leaving him 0.198s clear of Leclerc's Ferrari as Norris was less than three tenths adrift ahead of Sprint Qualifying later on Friday.

With just one hour in which to fine-tune set-ups and get to grips with the demanding Marina Bay Street Circuit, teams and drivers immediately headed out at 1630 local time, despite the dusty and sub-optimal track conditions.

Sparks were soon flying in the fading light as cars tackled the bumps, with Russell reporting that "the car feels very stiff" as the Mercedes driver prepares to start Sunday's Grand Prix from the back of the grid after power unit changes.

Drivers were soon exploring the limits, Lance Stroll's Aston Martin and Norris' McLaren taking to the run-off areas at Turns 1 and 16 respectively, with the majority of drivers initially running the hard Pirelli tyre.

By the 15-minute mark, Norris had whittled the fastest time down to a 1m 34.367s as track conditions improved and temperatures marginally dropped into the evening.

title: Why Singapore Sprint weekend is such a challenge for drivers
excerpt:
Like any street race venue, Singapore has always been a big test for Formula 1 drivers as they build up their speed and confidence over the weekend in the run-up to Qualifying.

And as a night race, there is always the extra challenge of not just the normal ramping up of grip that you get on any street track, but also the change in conditions associated with the move from daylight to darkness sessions.

Throw in the heat and punishing night race schedule, with its early morning finishes for drivers and team members, and Singapore is one of the toughest events on the schedule.

This year the Sprint format has added a further dimension. Everyone has just the Friday FP1 session with which to get their eye in before plunging into Sprint Qualifying – thus they will have to get up to limit a lot earlier than they usually do at a street venue, which inevitably creates some risk.

Add in the fact that the single practice session will be held in the daytime, Sprint Qualifying that follows is at night, and then the Sprint itself is set to take place in sunshine, and it won’t be easy for anyone to hit the set-up sweet spot that is ideal for all circumstances.

“It’s going to be very interesting,” says World Championship leader Kimi Antonelli. “First of all, a Sprint weekend in a city circuit is always very challenging, because the track just evolves so quickly that it's going to be so different from session to session.

“Also, FP1 tomorrow is going to be in the day, and Quali is going to be in the night. So it's going to be very, very different. But it's a good challenge for us drivers, for the team.”

Coping with changing grip conditions will be the key, and Max Verstappen believes it is important to start from a good baseline in practice.

“As every year here, you know that during the day you have a little bit less grip,” says the Sepang winner. “It's probably a little bit harder on the tyres. But the most important thing is just to find a good balance with the car straight away in FP1. That will probably just help a lot for the rest of your weekend.

“It's always hectic, a Sprint weekend, to make the right choices. And sometimes you just have a better one, or you have a bit more of a more straightforward one than others. But at the moment, it's very difficult to know how it's going to go.

“But yeah, naturally, when you drive during the day at a Sprint compared to in the night, it will have different challenges. But at the same time, we also know that this track is very hard to pass.

“So I think at the end of the day, the most important thing is qualifying for Sprint, or the race, because that normally defines where you finish.”

Just as some drivers take more time to get up to speed, some teams have a better record of arriving with a car suited to a given track. Lewis Hamilton is confident that Ferrari fall into that category and can thus count on being strong from FP1 onwards.

“I honestly think we generally hit the ground often running pretty well, more often than not, in FP1,” says the seven-time World Champion. “And then from session to session, some people close up, some people pull away. But I think our simulation team did a really great job, and more often than not, the car started in a not a terrible place throughout the year.

“So I'm hoping that we start from the right place, and it's exciting to come here, to come to Singapore, and you only have one session. Everyone's in the same boat, so it could be good, could be not good. But we'll see how it goes tomorrow.”

Russell promises 'all-out attack' in Singapore amid penalty

Alex Albon echoes the theme of starting with a solid set-up, and he makes an interesting observation about the day/night changes.

“It’s not so much the temperature, but it's what the sun does to the tyres as it comes out and goes down,” says the Williams driver. “So what you'll see normally in FP1 and FP3, the tyres are quite easy to get up to temperature and get them to work. And as soon as the sun drops, the tyres take on a completely different response. But we're used to that because that's been here every year.

“In terms of set-up changes, you kind of go into this weekend with a little bit more of a baseline, something that kind of we know will work, something that that fits most tracks.

“Most probably, you go on the side of confidence, whether that's through ride, suspension, just general set-up being a little bit more understeer, and then you kind of try to build the weekend a little bit differently like that.”

The schedule is the same for everyone, but it will be an especially tough test for Arvid Lindblad as the only rookie in the field.

The Briton has had to learn other tracks on Sprint weekends already this season, but he agrees that Singapore will be particularly tricky.

“It's just a normal tendency of the night races that you do have some sessions a little bit more in the daylight,” says the Racing Bulls driver. “So you don't have that similarity across the five sessions, let's say. Yes, that's an added challenge.

“I would say that maybe I can relate a bit more to F2. I'd have to have a look to the last year to have a look at how much the lap times improved.

"It was very often in F2 when we’d do a practice during the day on the hard [tyre], and then you’d go to Qualifying at night on the soft, and you go like five seconds quicker.

“I don't think it'll be that much here, but I've had it where you go back out and you have a load more grip, and you have to just get on it.”

That building up of confidence on a wall-lined track will be harder for Lindblad than anyone else, given that thus far he has only seen it in the simulator.

“You still can build up, but it's obviously a very different way you have to do that,” he says. “I experienced that in Canada. I really tried to make an effort in the first run to just build up the confidence and get comfortable, and then you start to push on towards the last laps of FP1, and then more in Sprint Quali.

“It's true that it's not easy because on street circuits, it is all about building up. In the end, all that matters is that you go into Qualifying confident and comfortable.

“And I didn't do the best job of that in the previous two street circuits; I crashed twice in FP2. But obviously I can learn from that, and it was a valuable lesson. But it's even harder now on a Sprint weekend, because you have even fewer sessions. So it's something I'm thinking about – how to get that balance right.”

Verstappen cautious about chances of victory

Given his victory in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was his first of the season, extending his run of winning at least one race a season to 11 years, it's perhaps understandable that Verstappen didn't want to get carried away with his chances of making it back-to-back victories.

title: Why splitting car specs is a 'no-brainer' for Mercedes
excerpt:
Mercedes have committed to an unusual strategy for the Singapore Grand Prix, as it will field its two W17s with completely different aero packages over what will already be a hectic and complicated Sprint weekend.

While Kimi Antonelli will stick with the updates as seen in Sepang last weekend, George Russell will revert to the previous version, thus giving the team a direct back-to-back comparison over all three days of the event.

Mercedes have taken this approach because the results produced by the new updates, which were introduced in Malaysia, proved to be inconclusive.

It was hardly a disaster, given that Antonelli finished second and Russell was destined for the podium before his late retirement, but the feeling in the camp was that it didn’t produce the lap time benefits anticipated.

Russell floated the idea of using Singapore as a back-to-back test even before the Sepang race, but his retirement guaranteed him a power unit grid penalty for this weekend, making the decision an obvious one.

“I instigated the conversation prior to the race on Sunday,” he said on Thursday's media day in Singapore. “So when the failure happened, it was kind of a no-brainer, because we were kind of 50-50 about it pre-race. And I was more in favour to do it, and that was even pre-race. Whereas now it is a total no-brainer.”

Russell may well find out that he has drawn the short straw, but it’s a risk that he is willing to take and he sees a bigger picture of helping the team to draw firm conclusions about the new parts.

“I think for any team, it's always very important,” he said. “However, there's no signs telling us the upgrade was not working, and we know the car we had in Baku was the same car as we had in Budapest and Zandvoort, and in Baku we were on pole by eight-tenths, and in Budapest, we were four-tenths off the pace.

“So those fluctuations, even with a consistent car and your rivals with the same car, are drastic. You have a fluctuation plus or minus one second, it can be, that delta. So we're pretty confident it's Malaysia specific.

“When you look at the pace of Red Bull as well, they clearly over performed compared to where they've been this season compared to all of the other teams, and actually, when you look at our pace compared to McLaren and Ferrari, it wasn't too dissimilar. It wasn't like massively out of bed.

“So this engine penalty this weekend has just given a good opportunity to roll back. It's the car that I won in Baku with – so let's see.”

Russell promises 'all-out attack' in Singapore amid penalty

In addition to the parts seen in Sepang, Antonelli also has a new front wing in Singapore, which in effect completes the update package but it remains to be seen whether or not that’s the key that makes it come alive.

The Italian acknowledges that last weekend the updates didn’t produce the expected gains in Malaysia.

“Of course, the numbers are a different story in Sepang,” said the Italian. “But I think Sepang, it was a bit of an outlier because the tarmac was just so rough. Actually, in some corners we were missing tarmac, and also it was so hot. We had at times 60-plus degree track temperatures, so I think was a bit of an outlier.

“And definitely I feel like this weekend is going to be a bit more representative. Cooler temperatures, the tarmac is in a much better state, and I think it's going to be a very good test, because in Sepang we struggled a lot in low-speed, and here we have a lot of low-speed.

“So let's see how it's going to be. And plus, we'll have two different cars on two different packages. So that is going to be interesting to see, we're going to have a straight comparison on that side.”

Antonelli has no qualms about sticking with the updates, and believes Singapore will get the best out of them.

“Well, I didn't really get to decide,” he said. “It was it was mainly the team that decided to go back on the old package. As I said before, we think it was it was an outlier, and we do believe the new package can work well. It's just a matter of trying to put the car in the right window, and understand it more.

“And this weekend, I think, is a good example. It's going to be a good opportunity to see and to compare the two packages. And because we know the old one, we've known it for ages, we know how to set up the car around that package. We know it works really well, and is really fast in these kinds of tracks. And we really want to understand.

“On the other hand, this new package and trying to really strike the maximum out of it, because the team has done a tremendous job. They've put in so much work on this new package, and it would be just a shame to write it off so early.

“So I feel like I'm quite comfortable on keeping it – and actually I really want to help the team out to understand it more, and as I said before try to extract the potential.”

title: Carlos Sainz hits out at FIA over perceived lack of 'sporting equity'
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has voiced his dissatisfaction with the FIA over what he perceives to be a lack of "sporting equity" from motorsport's governing body.

Sainz implied bias was at play over some recent decisions taken, making reference to a call made last weekend at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

After the chaos on the formation lap at the Sepang International Circuit, the FIA opted to start the race in the original grid order, despite the regulations suggesting that the new, jumbled-up positions should have been used to determine who starts where once racing did eventually get underway.

Due to the disarray that took place on account of the "software bug" that plagued some cars, it was felt that common sense prevailed, with numerous cars displaced from their original positions and cars split across multiple laps.

Fast forward to sprint qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix, an "unfortunate human error" during SQ1 meant that Overtake Mode was not activated once the session resumed following a Sergio Perez-induced red flag.

The FIA confirmed that it was subsequently turned on, but after just 27 seconds, it was actively disabled again, to try to preserve sporting fairness.

However, in doing so, this advantaged some drivers over others. Sainz, who qualified P22 and last under the lights at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, was not one of those, so was consequently disadvantaged — to the tune of half a second.

"Unfortunately, we had a really poor lap there," Sainz said after SQ1 in Singapore. "We only got one lap, and we had some issues with the brakes in FP1; we had to change them... [and] we were still having some brake issues — had a few lockups, struggling a lot with that and with the tyres."

Turning his attention to the issue at hand, which has since been confirmed to be the result of human error in race control, Sainz, who is also a Grand Prix Drivers' Association (GDPA) director, added: "But, on top of that, half of the cars did the lap with half a second quicker engine than the others.

"There was another software issue with the cars. This time around, we were on the bad end of it."

Sainz sees inconsistencies

Sainz was aggrieved by the FIA decision-making process seemingly advantaging bigger teams and drivers, with none of the headline names affected by the mistake in race control during SQ1.

"And for whatever reason, the FIA, like in Malaysia, didn't decide to do sporting equity, and were happy to do half of the cars in qualifying with a higher power than the other half of the cars," the four-time grand prix winner added.

"So a bit confused why the sport keeps doing different things depending on who is out in Q1 or who is out in Lap 1."

The Williams driver also stood to gain considerably after the disorder of the formation lap in Sepang, when the FIA decided to revert the grid order and nullify any changes in position.

At the time, Lewis Hamilton — who had qualified second alongside polesitter Max Verstappen — was the biggest name to be handed the reprieve, playing directly into Sainz's remarks.

title: Lewis Hamilton takes blame for crucial Singapore sprint qualifying mistake
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has taken the blame for an error during sprint qualifying, which he feels may have impacted his final result.

Hamilton ended the session in sixth place, marking a difficult result for him as he was outpaced by team-mate Charles Leclerc in third.

The seven-time champion was among a small handful of cars that opted to set an early lap during SQ3, rather than wait until the dying moments of the session when the track condition was at its peak.

It was a choice that Hamilton himself made, and suggested that it played a role in his lacklustre result.

“It was looking good in Q1 and Q2, and then I don't really know where it went away,” Hamilton said.

“We did a slightly different run plan to the others. It was my choice, and I think I got that wrong.”

Hamilton lacked tyre confidence in SQ3

However, he also acknowledged that the switch over to soft tyres for SQ3 brought its own challenges, having felt more comfortable on the mediums in the first two segments.

“But ultimately, just the car was very oversteery on that lap,” he said. “I don't know if the rears were not ready or if they're overheating.

“It was difficult to say, but it was very, very snappy, oversteery, and it just wasn't a good lap overall.

“On the mediums, it was good. Just much different on the softs, lots of grip, but only on the front and none at the rear.

“It could be balance, but ultimately I had the pace in the first two sessions, and then all of a sudden I didn't have the grip on the rear for some reason on that last lap.”

title: FIA reveal 'unfortunate human error' further influenced sprint qualifying
excerpt:
The FIA has reported that an "unfortunate human error" in race control meant Overtake Mode was unavailable after the red flag stoppage in SQ1 at the Singapore Grand Prix.

This issue was unrelated to the problems with F1's timing system during the first segment of sprint qualifying at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

However, it may have influenced the outcome of SQ1, with the motorsport governing body confirming that once the oversight was identified, Overtake Mode was reactivated for a period of 27 seconds before again being disabled.

The series of events occurred after the session was resumed following the Sergio Perez-induced red flag interruption.

"During the first period of Sprint Qualifying, there was a human error in Race Control unrelated to the timing issue also encountered in SQ1," the FIA said in a statement.

"This issue in question meant Overtake Mode was not available after the red flag period during SQ1. When it became apparent that Overtake Mode was not active after the restart, it was then activated for a period of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.

"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap.

"The second and third periods of Sprint Qualifying were not affected."

It is not clear whether — or the extent to which — any cars were disadvantaged due to the problem, and which cars were able to access the added power that comes with Overtake Mode for those 27 seconds.

However, Carlos Sainz, who qualified last, has claimed he lost half a second. And Lawrence Stroll has claimed son Lance lost six tenths of a second.

The situation also explains why cars were not able to go faster than Lewis Hamilton's early benchmark time once the session resumed.

title: Max Verstappen voices Red Bull shock as Singapore sprint pole in doubt
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has admitted surprise over the performance of his Red Bull car during sprint qualifying after taking pole position for Saturday's race.

However, his result is under threat as he faces a stewards' investigation for allegedly overtaking under yellow flag conditions.

Verstappen entered the Singapore weekend on a high after taking his first race win of the year last time out in Sepang.

Continuing where he left off, Verstappen beat George Russell to the top of the timesheet by one-tenth of a second, marking the first time he has topped a sprint qualifying session this year.

“It's always close here in Singapore, and also your lap, you're pushing as hard as you think is possible, close to the walls in places,” he said.

“Once we bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more.

“But I did not expect this, so of course, I'm very happy to be first.”

Verstappen will visit the stewards after moving in front of Lewis Hamilton during SQ1 through a yellow flag zone, which was deployed due to debris on the track.

However, with an investigation looming, Verstappen commended the work undertaken by Red Bull at recent events to improve its car.

“The last few races we have been a lot stronger,” he said.

“But of course, this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car.

“But we managed to drive with them as well as possible.”

title: Max Verstappen stuns in sprint qualifying but pole under threat from investigation
excerpt:
Max Verstappen stormed to pole position for the sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix, but could face a grid penalty for a potential yellow flag infringement.

Max Verstappen clinched pole position for the sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix, besting George Russell by just over a tenth of a second under the lights of the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Charles Leclerc rounded out the top three, ahead of the McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris.

Verstappen's pole is, however, at risk. The Red Bull driver is under investigation for an alleged yellow flag infringement during SQ1.

Lewis Hamilton, whom the Dutchman passed on track under those conditions, reported his old foe over team radio, with the stewards opting for a closer look after the session.

There were two notable delays to proceedings. First, Sergio Perez crashed during SQ1, which ultimately culminated in the red flag coming out after his limping Cadillac left debris strewn across the track surface.

Secondly, problems with the F1 timing system during the same segment confused the order. Although who survived and who was eliminated was eventually corrected, there was a pause to ensure the issue was fixed, meaning SQ2 started only a few minutes before SQ3 was scheduled to end.

Verstappen overcame an ERS issue before the sprint qualifying, with Red Bull making precautionary changes to his RB22.

The times came tumbling down when the eight minutes of SQ3 got going. Instantly, Norris went one second quicker than in SQ2, underlining the rapid rates of track evolution at F1's original night race.

Leclerc, Russell and the McLarens looked to be in the hunt for pole, but it was Verstappen who would prevail.

The 29-year-old, who was late out with work being undertaken on his car, eventually set a pole time of 1:31.156, which was 1.6 seconds quicker than his own SQ2 time.

Sprint Qualifying 2

After a short delay due to problems with the timing system, SQ2 got underway, with the Ferrari duo of Leclerc and Hamilton setting the early pace.

Russell struggled in his Mercedes, sitting down in eighth and having to bail out of his second effort after locking his tyres.

The British driver managed to survive with his final run, however, vaulting out of the danger zone to fourth-quickest in the middle segment.

Despite that late scare for the Mercedes driver, there were no surprise eliminations from SQ2.

Verstappen was keen to point out potentially being impeded by Hamilton during his last effort, as the two old adversaries continued to fight it out on track.

The opening 12-minute session saw most cars immediately file out onto the circuit, but just before the halfway mark, Sergio Perez's crash at Turn 4 triggered the first red flag of the weekend.

Initially, the incident brought out yellow flags, but as he attempted to drag his ailing Cadillac back to the pits, he left debris strewn all over the track.

That left numerous drivers, including the Red Bulls and McLarens, without a time on the board, and the prospect of a high-intensity, compressed end to SQ1.

Verstappen was noted for a potential yellow flag infringement, having passed Hamilton on track. The Ferrari driver was quick to flag it to his team, whilst the Dutchman radioed Red Bull to attempt to defend his case.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion will be investigated after the conclusion of sprint qualifying. The stewards, meanwhile, declined to further look into Perez for potentially driving his car in an unsafe condition.

Once the segment resumed, it was fairly business as usual, with no shock exits to report. However, the issues with the F1 timing tower meant it was initially unclear that Gabriel Bortoleto survived at the expense of Arvid Lindblad.

title: Bizarre timing issue sparks Singapore GP sprint qualifying drama
excerpt:
An unusual issue during sprint qualifying in Singapore has caused confusion and drama, resulting in a delay to the start of SQ2.

Towards the end of SQ1, the timing boards sparked uncertainty when they did not register the correct information as the drivers crossed the line.

It created an uncertain picture as to who had actually progressed into the second part of the session, and who was out of the running.

After several minutes, the timing boards suddenly updated, marking a considerable delay to the point in which the elimination order is normally confirmed.

The confusion prompted a delay to the start of SQ2, which got underway almost 20 minutes after the chequered flag was waved in SQ1.

A statement delivered by the FIA confirmed that the “start of SQ2 will be delayed due to an issue with timing systems, some lap times had not been registered. That is now resolved and the current timings are considered correct.”

While the session was able to resume, the FIA had cast doubt on that possibility, ending its statement with: “We are investigating whether we can proceed with the rest of the session.”

title: Max Verstappen under investigation after Singapore GP sprint quali infringement
excerpt:
Max Verstappen will face the Singapore Grand Prix stewards following an apparent infringement during sprint qualifying.

The incident came after a crash involving Cadillac's Sergio Perez at the Marina Bay Street Circuit in SQ1. The Mexican driver crunched the nose of his car into a wall at Turn 4, leading to initial yellow flags

Although Perez managed to reverse and return to the track, double-waved yellows were shown as debris was deposited on the circuit.

At one point under the yellows, Verstappen passed Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who had set the fastest time when the session was ultimately red-flagged to allow the marshals to clear away the bits of carbon fibre from the Cadillac.

"Max overtook me under a yellow flag," radioed Hamilton to his team.

Verstappen responded over his radio, saying he did so as a precaution given the circumstances.

The stewards will now hear the argument from the four-time F1 champion as to why he committed a clear offence.

Verstappen went on to finish quickest in SQ1 with a lap of one minute 33.477s, 0.018s ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

title: Sergio Perez crash sparks first Singapore Grand Prix red flag
excerpt:
A crash for Sergio Perez caused the first red flag of the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, marking a setback for the Mexican and the Cadillac team.

Perez locked up into Turn 4 shortly after the start of the session, causing damage to his front wing.

As Perez peeled back to the pit lane under his own power, the front wing got lodged under his car before being ripped from the structure altogether.

It then disintegrated into many pieces, prompting race control to deploy a red flag and stop the session to clean up the track.

Perez was subsequently noted for driving the car in an unsafe condition, before no further action was taken.

The Mexican enters the race weekend hoping for a notable result, stating that it was likely Cadillac's last chance this year to score points.

The incident caused scrutiny elsewhere on the grid as Lewis Hamilton called out Max Verstappen for allegedly overtaking him under yellow flags as they drove past the scene of Perez's stricken front wing.

title: George Russell makes 'total no-brainer' claim after sparking crucial Mercedes talks
excerpt:
George Russell has described it as a "total no-brainer" for Mercedes to revert him to an older specification for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, while insisting the team has seen nothing to suggest its Malaysia upgrade failed to work.

The upgrade, introduced at Sepang, had been designed to boost downforce through the medium- and high-speed corners. But Russell retired from third place at the Bahrain Grand Prix with a power unit issue, five laps from the finish, and has now been hit with a grid penalty for taking an additional power unit element beyond his seasonal allocation.

That penalty has handed Mercedes the opportunity to run a direct comparison in Singapore, with Russell switching back to the aerodynamic package he used to win in Azerbaijan, while Kimi Antonelli continues with the upgraded specification introduced in Malaysia.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Russell, who finished quickest in the sole practice session in Singapore, played down suggestions the new parts were the problem.

"For any team, it's always very important," said Russell. "However, there's no sign telling us the upgrade was not working. The car we had in Baku was the same car as we had in Budapest and Zandvoort.

"In Baku, we were on pole by eight tenths, and then in Budapest, we were four tenths off the pace. So those fluctuations, even with a consistent car and your rivals with the same car, are drastic. Plus or minus one second, it can be that delta.

"So we're pretty confident it's Malaysia-specific. When you look at the pace of Red Bull as well, they clearly over-performed compared to where they've been this season, compared to all of the other teams.

"And actually, when you look at our pace compared to McLaren and Ferrari, it wasn't too dissimilar. It wasn't like massively out of bed. So this engine penalty this weekend's just given a good opportunity to roll back. It's a car that I won in Baku with, so let's see."

George Russell confirms remarkable timing of Mercedes conversations

Russell revealed that the decision to return to the old specification in Singapore was not a reaction to his Sepang retirement, but a conversation he had already started with Mercedes beforehand.

Asked how involved he was in those discussions, the 28-year-old explained that the matter had already been under debate within the team prior to his power unit failure.

Russell revealed: "Well, I instigated the conversation prior to the race on Sunday, so when the failure happened, it was kind of a no-brainer because we were kind of 50-50 about it pre-race.

"I was more in favour of doing it, and that was even pre-race. Whereas now, it is a total no-brainer."

title: Toto Wolff bashes 'brainless' F1 fans over 'hilarious' Mercedes claims
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has taken aim at the "brainless" accusations that Mercedes favours Kimi Antonelli over George Russell in decisions taken at Mercedes throughout the F1 season.

Wolff vehemently defended his team, calling such suggestions "completely nonsensical" after a fresh volley of allegations online following the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, where Russell suffered a power unit failure.

The British driver has experienced considerable bad luck this year, but the misfortune has not been isolated to his half of the Mercedes garage.

Kimi Antonelli has been hit by issues at times, notably in Spain and at Silverstone, and critical reliability problems have plagued the young Italian and Russell in two grands prix apiece.

It must be said that Russell has experienced more niggling issues on his W17, but that alone does not explain his 84-point deficit to his team-mate in the F1 drivers' standings.

The 28-year-old has struggled for pace more often, and there has been a clear performance gap between the pair for much of the campaign.

"They're brainless, whoever thinks that," Wolff told media, including RacingNews365. "It's completely nonsensical.

"We've had it in the past with Lewis fans... like literally, I don't know what's going on? Do they think I have a button that says 'George engine failure now', or that I'm disadvantaging one driver against the other when we're fighting for a constructors' championship?"

Wolff says he is 'Satan' to some vocal critics online

After the six-time constructors' champions struggled with its latest upgrade package at the Sepang International Circuit, Russell and Antonelli will do an A/B test between the old specification car and the new one in Singapore.

That back-to-back profile will help the team establish which direction to develop in for next year and how it integrates the new parts for the rest of the current season.

Russell will take the old spec which won in Madrid and Baku for the weekend at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, whilst Antonelli will try and tame the new.

"We've always had the mindset of providing everybody with equal material, but I guess this is maybe where social media goes today," Wolff insisted before making light of some of the criticisms levied towards him online.

"People hide behind their screens, and then they lash out. There's a lot of polarisation going on.

"Sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they're abusing the team or me. I'm Satan, I've heard. So, overall, funny."

The justification for the split approach lies in large part due to Russell being consigned to the back of the pack under the lights of the Southeast Asian city-state.

Antonelli took a grid penalty to replenish his power unit component pool at the Italian Grand Prix, where he won from P19 on the grid.

The plan for Russell was to take his corresponding grid drop over the Americas triple-header, to tie in with the arrival of the Brackley-based team's ADUO upgrade.

Due to the nature of the various reliability problems each driver has suffered, Antonelli can change elements without needing to take an additional grid penalty, whereas Russell will face a "double whammy", in the words of Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord, meaning the Briton will start at the back of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix and also incur a grid drop when racing resumes in North America later this month.

"But really, zero understanding and respect for people who come up with these things," Wolff added. "They should, rather than watching Formula 1, they should do Teletubbies, or I don't know, some Mickey Mouses."

title: Red Bull confirm problem for Max Verstappen in Singapore
excerpt:
Max Verstappen suffered a radio failure during opening practice for the Singapore Grand Prix, Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies has confirmed.

The Dutchman's first running at Marina Bay did not go smoothly as he completed 22 laps during the session, among the fewest of anyone.

He was forced to return to the pits after just seven laps into the session on the hard tyre, with mechanics spotted working on the car.

Mekies explained the problem while the session was still ongoing, detailing that Verstappen had lost radio contact with the pit wall, leaving race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase unable to communicate with his driver.

Discussing the issue, Mekies told Sky F1: “We had no radio with Max in the first run which makes everyone's lives a bit difficult.

“That's why you see him out of the car as we are trying to fix the radio.”

[Article continues below]

Mekies voices Red Bull caution

Verstappen ended the FP1 outing in sixth, having opted not to run the soft tyres like his rivals ahead of him.

The Dutchman enters the weekend on the back of winning his first race of the year last time out in Sepang.

With Red Bull enjoying a strong step-up in form of late, Mekies insisted that nothing is guaranteed at a fresh event.

“The trend is positive,” he said. “Monza, Madrid, Baku, Malaysia there's been a bit more performance extracted from the car every time.

"Does it mean we have a seat to fight for victory in all races? No such thing is guaranteed and we have seen many examples this year of performance variations track to track.

“We have four teams very close to each other.

"We think we will be in the good group at all races but then it's down to extracting everything."

title: Lando Norris reveals true cost of painful and mysterious McLaren issue
excerpt:
Lando Norris has been hamstrung by a mysterious problem plaguing the Mercedes power unit in the back of his McLaren.

Lando Norris has revealed the mystery straight-line speed deficit ailing his McLaren has cost him "two or three positions" in each of the last two qualifying sessions.

McLaren continues to investigate the problem, which was only affecting Norris' car and not team-mate Oscar Piastri's, but believes it has fixed the faulty components and that everything should be okay at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The issue first surfaced in Baku and resurfaced in Sepang, with Norris losing out purely on the straights while matching or outperforming Piastri through the corners.

McLaren estimated the deficit at around one to two tenths of a second per lap, caused by a small but consistent loss of top speed in power-limited sections of the circuit.

Team principal Andrea Stella monitored the situation closely alongside McLaren's power unit partner, Mercedes High Performance Powertrains, though the exact cause has not been disclosed.

"We should say that the issue we see on Lando's car is about a lack of straight-line speed," Stella said at the time to explain the nature of the problem.

"So we see that in the power-limited section, the car accelerates a little less and develops a little bit less top speed, all the other parameters being the same. We talk about probably between one and two kph; they are small quantities."

"We can quantify even a lap time loss that I would say in excess of one-tenth of a second, possibly between one and two tenths of a second, and a different conversation is about why that is, and while we can talk immediately about a lack of power, in reality there can be different reasons."

Norris endured two 'frustrating' weekends

McLaren believes it has resolved the issue for the weekend at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where the problem would have been less consequential anyway.

Asked whether he expected everything to be back to normal for the Singapore Grand Prix, Norris told media including RacingNews365: "Yeah, hopeful... It's obviously also a circuit where straights are not the highest priority and not as detrimental as the last few weekends."

"But nevertheless, you always want to go down the straights as quickly as you should be able to. And it's always tough when you come out of corners better and end up going slower."

"So, it's been a frustrating two weekends trying to figure out what the issue's been and why there's just been a constant lack of straight-line speed and performance."

Norris made clear just how costly the problem has been in a championship fight where small margins matter, even if — sitting fifth in the standings and 132 points adrift of Kimi Antonelli — his F1 drivers' title defence is all but over.

"And especially in this kind of battle we've been in, the last two qualifyings it's been two or three positions," Norris added. "So, it's cost me quite a lot."

"At the same time, there's obviously things I can do better as well. But confident that the team have done a good job."

"They put a lot of work into trying to figure things out, and I'm hopeful that it'll be better this weekend..."

title: George Russell puts PU misery behind him to spearhead sole Singapore GP practice
excerpt:
George Russell finished quickest in the sole practice session ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix.

On soft rubber, Russell posted a time of one minute 32.274s in his Mercedes, finishing 0.198s ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, with Lando Norris in his McLaren a further 0.075s further back.

Russell, however, will start at the back of the grid. During the session, the FIA confirmed Mercedes had fitted a completely new power unit, comprising ICE, turbocharger, MGU-K, energy store, control electronics and exhaust set.

The Briton has also reverted to a car specification that helped him dominate the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, with Antonelli using the upgrade which was on the W17s for last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, allowing Mercedes to comparison test the different packages.

[Article continues below]

With only one practice session before the first sprint qualifying session over a Singapore weekend, all the drivers wasted little time taking to a very dusty track.

Following several sighter laps, Red Bull's Verstappen set the opening respectable time of 1:35.641s on the hard tyre, a time quickly usurped by Leclerc by just over four-tenths of a second, before Russell became the first to dip below 95 seconds.

As the track rapidly ramped up, Norris comfortably slashed six-tenths of a second off Russell's time with a 1:34.367s. That was not the leading one for long, however, as Leclerc posted a 1:33.969s.

Russell, though, soon shaved a tenth off that to take up top spot before Antonelli nipped ahead by 0.056s.

At the halfway stage, and with no change to the hard tyre running, Antonelli led Leclerc by 0.034s, followed by Russell. The Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was fourth quickest at that point, two-tenths of a second down.

Verstappen, who had encountered radio issues early in the session, according to team principal Laurent Mekies, was 1.1s adrift.

With 20 minutes remaining, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg became the weekend's first casualty, with his car grinding to a halt as he made his way along the start-finish straight, sparking a VSC.

The veteran German parked his car at the end of the pit lane, where marshals helped retrieve it and push it back into the garage. He did not return as his mechanics attended to the problem.

Inside the final 15 minutes, the drivers upped the ante on tyres, with a number switching to the mediums, mandatory in the first two sessions of sprint qualifying, whilst others swapped to the softs.

Russell was one of those on the red-striped rubber, going almost a second quicker than Antonelli's best on the hards, posting a 1:32.864s, only to be beaten by Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton by 0.043s.

Russell, though, was not to be denied, posting a time of almost six-tenths quicker than Hamilton before Leclerc and Norris separated the duo.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri completed the top five, who were all on softs, albeit 0.564s down.

Verstappen led the medium-tyre runners, 0.732s back, followed by Antonelli, who had a late off-track moment before reversing, Hadjar, Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Liam Lawson for Racing Bulls, the New Zealander 1.881s off the pace.

At the rear of the 22-car field were the Cadillacs of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, both just over three seconds down.

title: Brutal George Russell situation becomes reality as FIA confirm Mercedes changes
excerpt:
The FIA has confirmed the comprehensive power unit change Mercedes has made to George Russell's car after he retired from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Russell will have seven new components in the back of his W17 for the Singapore Grand Prix, consigning him to the back of the grid at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

In addition to a new internal combustion engine (ICE), Russell will have a new turbocharger (TC), exhaust set (EXH), motor generator unit-kinetic (MGU-K), energy store (ES) and control electronics unit (PU-CE).

As none of those components is within his existing allocation and has extended the pool, he will take a 10-place grid penalty for the first unit — as it will be his first power unit-related grid drop of the campaign — and a further five places for each of the rest.

He will also take an additional power unit ancillary component (PU-ANC), but that is only his fifth of six allowed.

Further adding to his misfortune, Mercedes has not been able to expedite its next ADUO upgrade, so Russell will be forced to take another grid penalty over the Americas triple header when that power unit update does arrive.

Deputy team principal Bradley Lord described the situation as a "double whammy" for the eight-time grand prix winner.

The British driver is currently 84 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli in the F1 drivers' championship standings, and can be expected to be even further behind after the round at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

With only five or six subsequent events remaining, Russell's title fight is essentially over.
